claim: The study included 288 ALS patients with up to 5-year follow-up during 2015-2020 recruited at the only tertiary referral center for ALS in Stockholm, Sweden.
source: Therefore, we conducted a longitudinal cohort study including 288 ALS patients with up to 5-year follow-up during 2015–2020 recruited at the only tertiary referral center for ALS in Stockholm, Sweden
evidence: The manuscript directly states the study design, sample size, follow-up duration, time period, and recruitment location.

claim: Leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased gradually over time since ALS diagnosis.
source: We found that leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased gradually over time since diagnosis
evidence: This finding is supported by longitudinal measurements and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes were negatively correlated with functional status.
source: We found that leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased gradually over time since diagnosis and were negatively correlated with functional status
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical correlations between these cell types and ALSFRS-R scores.

claim: Leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes were not associated with risk of death.
source: We found that leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased gradually over time since diagnosis and were negatively correlated with functional status, but not associated with risk of death
evidence: Cox model analysis showed no significant association with mortality.

claim: Leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes were not associated with disease progression rate.
source: We found that leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased gradually over time since diagnosis and were negatively correlated with functional status, but not associated with risk of death or disease progression rate
evidence: Statistical analysis found no significant correlation with progression rate.

claim: NK cells were negatively associated with risk of death (HR=0.61, 95% CI=[0.42-0.88] per SD increase).
source: For lymphocyte subpopulations, NK cells (HR= 0.61, 95% CI = [0.42–0.88] per SD increase) and Th2-diffrentiated CD4+ central memory T cells (HR= 0.64, 95% CI = [0.48–0.85] per SD increase) were negatively associated with risk of death
evidence: Cox model analysis provided hazard ratios with confidence intervals.

claim: Th2-differentiated CD4+ central memory T cells were negatively associated with risk of death (HR=0.64, 95% CI=[0.48-0.85] per SD increase).
source: For lymphocyte subpopulations, NK cells (HR= 0.61, 95% CI = [0.42–0.88] per SD increase) and Th2-diffrentiated CD4+ central memory T cells (HR= 0.64, 95% CI = [0.48–0.85] per SD increase) were negatively associated with risk of death
evidence: Cox model analysis provided hazard ratios with confidence intervals.

claim: CD4+ EMRA T cells were positively associated with risk of death (HR=1.39, 95% CI=[1.01-1.92] per SD increase).
source: while CD4+ effector memory cells re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA) T cells (HR= 1.39, 95% CI = [1.01–1.92] per SD increase) and CD8+ T cells (HR= 1.38, 95% CI = [1.03–1.86] per SD increase) were positively associated with risk of death
evidence: Cox model analysis provided hazard ratios with confidence intervals.

claim: CD8+ T cells were positively associated with risk of death (HR=1.38, 95% CI=[1.03-1.86] per SD increase).
source: while CD4+ effector memory cells re-expressing CD45RA (EMRA) T cells (HR= 1.39, 95% CI = [1.01–1.92] per SD increase) and CD8+ T cells (HR= 1.38, 95% CI = [1.03–1.86] per SD increase) were positively associated with risk of death
evidence: Cox model analysis provided hazard ratios with confidence intervals.

claim: None of the lymphocyte subpopulations was correlated with functional status or disease progression rate.
source: None of the lymphocyte subpopulations was correlated with functional status or disease progression rate
evidence: GEE model analysis found no significant correlations.

claim: Neutrophils and monocytes primarily reflect functional status in ALS.
source: Our findings suggest a dual role of immune cells in ALS prognosis, where neutrophils and monocytes primarily reflect functional status
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of associations found in the study.

claim: NK cells and different T lymphocyte populations act as prognostic markers for survival in ALS.
source: Our findings suggest a dual role of immune cells in ALS prognosis, where neutrophils and monocytes primarily reflect functional status whereas NK cells and different T lymphocyte populations act as prognostic markers for survival
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of associations found in the study.

claim: ALS is a rare but devastating neurodegenerative disease.
source: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rare but devastating neurodegenerative disease
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ALS.

claim: The etiology of ALS remains unknown for most patients.
source: Although a genetic cause has been demonstrated for some cases of ALS, the etiology remains unknown for most of the patients with ALS
evidence: This reflects current scientific understanding of ALS.

claim: There is currently no cure or effective treatment available for ALS.
source: There is currently no cure or effective treatment available for ALS
evidence: This is established knowledge about ALS treatment status.

claim: Neuroinflammatory features, including local glial activation and T-cell infiltration in the CNS, are well documented in ALS.
source: Neuroinflammatory features, including local glial activation and T-cell infiltration in the central nervous system (CNS), are well documented in ALS (Komine and Yamanaka, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Animal studies have demonstrated that altering the function of microglia and infiltrating T cells to the CNS affect disease progression in experimental ALS.
source: Animal studies have demonstrated that altering the function of microglia and infiltrating T cells to the CNS affect disease progression in experimental ALS (Beers et al., 2006; Martínez-Muriana et al., 2016; Beers et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Human studies have documented signs of systemic immune activation in ALS patients compared with healthy controls.
source: Human studies have also documented signs of systemic immune activation in ALS patients, compared with healthy controls, suggesting that peripheral immune activation may play a role in human ALS through the peripheral–central neuroimmune crosstalk (Liu et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Most previous studies on immune cells in ALS are not population based and have limited sample size.
source: Most of the previous studies (Jin et al., 2020; Rentzos et al., 2012; Henkel et al., 2012), however, are not population based and have limited sample size
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature with citations.

claim: Few studies have recorded immune cells longitudinally after ALS diagnosis.
source: Further, few studies have recorded immune cells longitudinally after ALS diagnosis, as most previous studies relied on a single measurement (Sheean et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous literature with a citation.

claim: The vast majority of cell populations in ALS patients were within the normal range, except for CD8+ CM cells, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells.
source: The vast majority of the cell populations were within the normal range, except for CD8+ central memory (CM) cells, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells, which were above the normal range
evidence: This is based on comparison with reference ranges.

claim: The levels of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased progressively over time, especially from 20 months after diagnosis onward.
source: In the main cohort, the levels of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased progressively over time, especially from 20 months after diagnosis onward (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal data and visualization in Figure 1.

claim: The temporal trends of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes were statistically significant with or without adjustment for age and sex.
source: These trends were statistically significant, with or without adjustment for age and sex, and remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing (Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: No clear temporal trend was noted for lymphocytes in ALS patients.
source: In contrast, no clear temporal trend was noted for lymphocytes
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis of lymphocyte counts.

claim: The levels of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased after Riluzole treatment compared with before such treatment.
source: The levels of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased, whereas the levels of lymphocytes decreased, after Riluzole treatment, compared with before such treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on comparison of cell counts before and after treatment.

claim: The levels of lymphocytes decreased after Riluzole treatment compared with before such treatment.
source: The levels of leukocytes, neutrophils, and monocytes increased, whereas the levels of lymphocytes decreased, after Riluzole treatment, compared with before such treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is based on comparison of cell counts before and after treatment.

claim: No clear temporal trend was noted for any lymphocyte subpopulation in the FlowC cohort.
source: In the FlowC cohort, no clear temporal trend was noted for any lymphocyte subpopulation
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis of lymphocyte subpopulations.

claim: ALS patients demonstrated persistently higher proportions of CD8+ CM, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+, and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells than the reference ranges.
source: although ALS patients demonstrated persistently higher proportions of CD8+ CM, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+, and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells than the reference ranges (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)

claim: After adjustment for age and sex, there was a decreasing % of naive CD4+ T cells since ALS diagnosis.
source: After adjustment for age and sex, there was a decreasing % of naive CD4+ T cells whereas increasing %s of CD4+ EMRA, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38− cells since ALS diagnosis (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is based on adjusted statistical analysis.

claim: After adjustment for age and sex, there were increasing %s of CD4+ EMRA, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38− cells since ALS diagnosis.
source: After adjustment for age and sex, there was a decreasing % of naive CD4+ T cells whereas increasing %s of CD4+ EMRA, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD8+HLA-DR+CD38− cells since ALS diagnosis (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is based on adjusted statistical analysis.

claim: Male patients showed lower levels of CD4+, naive CD4+, and Th2 of CD4+ CM cells compared with female patients.
source: Male patients showed lower levels of CD4+, naive CD4+, and Th2 of CD4+ CM cells, but higher levels of CD4+ effector memory (EM, CD4+ EMRA, CD8+, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells, compared with female patients, especially early stage after diagnosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4))

claim: Male patients showed higher levels of CD4+ EM, CD4+ EMRA, CD8+, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells compared with female patients.
source: Male patients showed lower levels of CD4+, naive CD4+, and Th2 of CD4+ CM cells, but higher levels of CD4+ effector memory (EM, CD4+ EMRA, CD8+, CD4+HLA-DR+CD38−, and CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells, compared with female patients, especially early stage after diagnosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4))
evidence: This is based on sex-stratified analysis.

claim: Patients with limb onset had lower levels of CD8+ CM and CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells compared with patients with other site of onset.
source: Patients with limb onset had lower levels of CD8+ CM and CD4+HLA-DR+CD38+ cells compared with patients with other site of onset
evidence: This is based on stratified analysis by site of onset.

claim: Carriers of C9orf72 expansions had higher levels of NK cells and T cells compared with other patients.
source: whereas carriers of C9orf72 expansions had higher levels of natural killer (NK) cells and T cells, but lower levels of naive CD4+ T cells and CD8+ EM cells, than other patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 5)

claim: Carriers of C9orf72 expansions had lower levels of naive CD4+ T cells and CD8+ EM cells compared with other patients.
